analysis.one_liner: Extends Social Security and Medicare payroll taxes to income above $400,000.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in the Senate Finance Committee and died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, wages stop counting toward Social Security taxes above a yearly cap (about $160,000), so people earning millions stop paying into the system early in the year. This bill would keep the Social Security tax going on earnings up to $400,000, add a 1.2% Medicare tax on income above $400,000 ($500,000 for couples), and sharply raise and broaden the 3.8% investment income tax — including on profits people take from businesses structured to avoid payroll taxes. The money would flow directly into the Social Security and Medicare trust funds, which face projected shortfalls in the coming decades.
analysis.who_benefits: Current and future Social Security and Medicare beneficiaries, whose trust funds would receive substantial new revenue from the highest-earning roughly 1% of taxpayers, extending the programs' solvency without benefit cuts or tax increases on anyone earning under $400,000.

how_it_helps.text: Applies the 12.4% Social Security tax to wages between the current annual cap and $400,000, so high earners keep contributing to the program for more of their income [S2][S3].
Adds a 1.2% Medicare tax on wages and self-employment income above $400,000 ($500,000 for joint filers) [S3].

Raises the tax on net investment income from 3.8% to 17.4% for people with income above $400,000, and expands it to cover active business profits that are currently exempt because they are paid out as business distributions rather than wages [S2][S3].
Routes the new revenue into the Social Security trust funds (71.3% to retirement and survivors, 10.3% to disability) and the Medicare hospital insurance trust fund (28.7%) [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Households earning more than $400,000 a year, and owners of pass-through businesses (partnerships, law firms, real estate and investment partnerships) who would no longer be able to avoid payroll taxes by taking income as business profits instead of wages.
analysis.who_pays_short: Households earning over $400,000 and pass-through business owners

drawbacks.text: High earners would pay substantially more: the combination of extended Social Security tax up to $400,000, the new 1.2% Medicare surtax, and a 17.4% investment income tax rate approaches a combined rate above 40% on some high incomes [S3].

Critics of lifting the payroll tax cap argue it changes Social Security's traditional structure as a benefit tied to contributions, and that raising taxes on business pass-through income can discourage investment and business formation — an argument supporters of the bill would need to answer.
The bill contains no benefit increase or solvency guarantee on its own; its effect depends entirely on the new revenue reaching the trust funds as designed [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs fall entirely on the top few percent of earners, while the benefit — more years of guaranteed Social Security and Medicare payments — reaches tens of millions of ordinary households. The main honest objection is the rate burden on high-income professionals and business owners and the broader economic effects of taxing pass-through profits, but those costs are concentrated while the gain is broad. The bill is a straightforward transfer from high earners to the two largest social insurance programs.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee in April 2023, and the committee never took it up; it died there when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse introduced the bill on April 18, 2023 with four Democratic cosponsors and no Republican support [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance the same day [S5].
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — and the bill expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: High earners and pass-through business owners are better off, since they never faced the new taxes; Social Security and Medicare trust funds gained no new revenue, and their projected shortfalls remain unaddressed.

industries.industry: Pass-through business owners (law firms, private equity, hedge funds, real estate partnerships)
industries.note: The bill would tax their active business profits under the payroll and investment income taxes, closing the gap where owners take income as distributions that escape payroll tax. Their gain under the status quo is a gap in the funding of programs ordinary workers pay into all year.

They would face extended Social Security taxes up to $400,000, a new 1.2% Medicare surtax, and a 17.4% investment income tax rate. Currently, high earners stop paying Social Security tax after the annual wage cap.
The Medicare hospital insurance trust fund would receive 28.7% of the new investment income tax, supporting payments to hospitals and coverage for beneficiaries.
